display_title: Higher Education in the AI Era
short_summary: As artificial intelligence reshapes entry-level tasks, academic institutions face urgent questions about how to prepare students for a rapidly evolving job market.

sources.name: Ynet
sources.title: תואר ביד, עבודה בסימן שאלה: מה באמת כדאי ללמוד בעידן ה-AI

paragraphs: The choice of an undergraduate degree has always involved a degree of uncertainty, requiring students to invest time and money while hoping employers will want to hire them upon graduation. However, in the era of artificial intelligence, a pressing question complicates this traditional gamble: how much of the work students are training for will be handled by automated tools by the time they finish their studies? Recently, NVIDIA CEO and founder Jensen Huang argued at the GTC Berlin 2026 conference that artificial intelligence will not terminate the profession of programming. Instead, he predicted that AI tools will actually increase the total number of individuals who write software. While this forecast offers a measure of optimism, it still leaves open questions regarding what these workers must learn and how educational institutions should train them today.

Concerns are particularly acute for individuals attempting to secure their first professional positions. Standard entry-level tasks such as drafting documents, gathering information, preparing presentations, and writing basic code traditionally serve as the primary stepping stones for beginners to learn their respective fields. Yet these are precisely the responsibilities that artificial intelligence tools can perform, at least partially. For employers, automation presents an opportunity to conserve time and resources. For recent graduates, however, it creates a formidable obstacle: how does one accumulate professional experience when the introductory tasks designed to ease newcomers into the industry are handed over to machines?

According to Dr. Ayelet Ben-Ezra Gelbard, CEO of Reichman University, universities must look far beyond simply adding a single standalone artificial intelligence course to their existing curricula. She asserts that the true risk facing modern education is not the total disappearance of specific professions, but rather the failure of academic institutions to adapt. Training young people as though the labor market has remained static is a dangerous miscalculation. Rather than avoiding entire fields of study, students should focus on developing critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving abilities, interpersonal communication, continuous learning habits, and AI literacy.

Furthermore, the evolution of entry-level roles presents a paradox for modern organizations. Historically, junior employees learned their trades through basic, repetitive assignments. If artificial intelligence assumes these introductory responsibilities, companies risk cutting off the pipeline that produces senior experts and managers in the future. Consequently, the challenge for employers is not whether to hire junior staff, but rather how to redesign these roles. The junior employee of tomorrow will likely spend less time on routine technical tasks and more time collaborating alongside AI systems, formulating problems, operating tools, evaluating outputs, and exercising human judgment.

To remain relevant during this profound period of economic transition, forward-thinking universities are transforming themselves into living laboratories for higher education. Reichman University, for instance, has implemented wide-ranging reforms and introduced new degree structures designed to foster interdisciplinary thinking and agility. Among these initiatives is the MAHAR program, a multi-disciplinary social science degree that allows students to build flexible study tracks. Experts emphasize that the ultimate advantage of human workers lies not merely in technical knowledge, but in multidisciplinary perspective, critical analysis, and the capacity to adapt swiftly to change.

Despite the disruption brought by advanced technology, traditional disciplines like computer science retain significant value, albeit with altered teaching methodologies. Rather than focusing strictly on syntax and manual coding, computer science education must now emphasize system comprehension, computational logic, and problem formulation. As automated tools generate more code, the value of professionals who understand complex systems and define correct problems increases proportionally. To prepare students effectively, academic institutions must integrate practical experience directly into their coursework, foster continuous learning, and update curricula to match the realities of a changing world.

facts.fact: Jensen Huang, CEO and founder of NVIDIA, stated at the GTC Berlin 2026 conference that artificial intelligence will not end programming, but rather increase the number of people who write software using new tools.
Dr. Ayelet Ben-Ezra Gelbard, CEO of Reichman University, noted that the real risk is not the disappearance of professions, but continuing to train young people as if the labor market has not changed.
Reichman University established the multi-disciplinary social sciences degree program known as the MAHAR program.
